flashcards.q: What is a Cook Reduction (Polynomial-Time Turing Reduction)?
flashcards.a: A language A is Cook reducible to a language B if A can be decided by a polynomial-time oracle Turing machine equipped with an oracle for B.

flashcards.q: What is a Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS)?
flashcards.a: An approximation algorithm for an optimization problem that takes an error parameter epsilon > 0 and produces a solution within a (1 + epsilon) factor of the optimum in polynomial time for any fixed epsilon.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between disjoint (mutually exclusive) and independent events?
flashcards.a: Disjoint events cannot occur at the same time, meaning P(A and B) = 0. Independent events do not influence each other's occurrence, meaning P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B).

proofs.title: NP-Completeness Proof for the General Clique Problem
proofs.explanation: Proving that finding whether a graph contains a clique of a given size is NP-complete by showing it is in NP and reducing 3SAT to it.
steps: Verify that CLIQUE is in NP by taking a subgraph of vertices as a certificate and checking in polynomial time if all pairs are connected by an edge.
Map a 3SAT formula with m clauses to a graph where each literal becomes a vertex, grouping vertices into trios representing each clause.
Connect vertices with edges if they belong to different clauses and are not contradictory literals (e.g., x and not-x).
Observe that the 3SAT formula is satisfiable if and only if the constructed graph contains a clique of size m, completing the polynomial-time reduction.

proofs.title: Decidability and Complexity of the Fixed k-Clique Problem
proofs.explanation: Demonstrating the complexity bounds for finding a clique of a fixed, constant size k in a graph.
steps: Formulate an algorithm that systematically enumerates all possible subsets of vertices of size k from a graph with n vertices.
Calculate the total number of subsets to check using the binomial coefficient n choose k, which simplifies to O(n^k) combinations.
For each subset, verify in O(k^2) constant time whether an edge exists between every pair of vertices in the subset.
Conclude that because k is a fixed constant, the overall runtime O(k^2 * n^k) is strictly polynomial, making the fixed k-clique problem fixed-parameter tractable.

quiz.q: How do Cook reductions differ fundamentally from Karp (mapping) reductions?
options: Cook reductions allow multiple, adaptive queries to an oracle and negation of the results, whereas Karp reductions allow only a single polynomial-time function mapping.
Cook reductions can only be applied to problems already known to be in P.
Karp reductions allow the algorithm to run in exponential time if the oracle returns false.
quiz.feedback: Cook reductions utilize an oracle machine model allowing multiple adaptive checks, while Karp reductions are restricted to a single many-one structural transformation function.

quiz.q: If an approximation scheme has a runtime of O(n^(1/epsilon)), which class does it belong to?
options: It is an exact exponential-time algorithm
quiz.feedback: It is a PTAS because the runtime is polynomial in n for any fixed constant epsilon, but it is not an FPTAS because the exponent grows as epsilon approaches zero.

quiz.q: If two events A and B are independent and both have non-zero probabilities, can they ever be disjoint?
options: Yes, independence guarantees they will never happen together, which means they are disjoint.
No, because if they are independent, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B) > 0, whereas disjoint events require P(A and B) = 0.
Only if the sample space is infinite.
quiz.feedback: Independent events with non-zero probabilities always have a joint probability greater than zero, meaning they must overlap and cannot be disjoint.
